subject.gist: Marie and Charles enclosed a summer house in a greenhouse for year-round family life, gaining a rooftop playground but still waking to winter cold.

story.text: Marie and Charles wrap a summer house in an ordinary greenhouse so their family can live there all year. Taking off the house roof gives them a sheltered terrace for playing and relaxing, and Marie notices that a cold, rainy summer bothers her far less than it bothers her friends. She can drink morning coffee beside a fig tree without getting wet. Charles brings his engineering skills to a wastewater system that feeds planted beds. Winter still means warm slippers and lighting a fire: this is a home that follows the seasons. They keep experimenting, with storing summer heat for winter still waiting on money and time.

claims.text: A summer house enclosed in a greenhouse for year-round living.
The home is on the Stockholm archipelago.
The greenhouse footprint is nearly twice the home’s footprint.
At that time, more than ten years ago, the greenhouse cost about €80,000.
claims.doubt: The subtitled answer follows a greenhouse-cost question but does not define scope; the year is given only as more than ten years before filming.

claims.text: The home was built more than ten years before filming.
Glass thickness is 4 millimeters [0.157 inches].
The household is completely independent of city sewage.
Additional heating runs only from mid-October to the end of March instead of from the end of September to May, cutting off several months a year.
The enclosure is an ordinary commercially available greenhouse.
Bengt Warne designed the greenhouse.
Bengt Warne began designing the first Naturhus in 1974.
Warne’s Nature House ideas are associated with the 1990s.
claims.doubt: The transcript dates the ideas to the 1990s; the description clarifies book-era influence and gives 1974 for the first design.

claims.text: A vacant-lot search became a purchase with an existing house.
The greenhouse preceded enlargement of the enclosed house.
The reconstructed timber exterior received only linseed oil.
The exterior was reconstructed a few years before filming.
The greenhouse keeps rain and wind off the house.
Retaining solar energy reduces the amount of insulation needed.
Removing the house roof created an additional living terrace.
Roof vents open and close automatically with temperature.
The house receives southern sun all day.
Without sun, greenhouse temperature is nearly the same as outdoors.
For example at the end of January it can be −2°C [28.4°F] outside and 15–20°C [59–68°F] upstairs.
Even in this greenhouse it gets cold in winter: at −20°C [−4°F] outside it gets maybe −10°C [14°F] in here, so some insulation and heating are still needed.
The cold season runs from late October to early April.
Fig trees do not survive freezing temperatures outdoors here.
The fig tree has many fruits this year.
Almost all glazing, including everything overhead, is security glass.
If broken, the security glass breaks into tiny pieces.
The household makes juice from its grapes.
Underground rainwater collection supplies plant watering.
No chemicals are added to the sewage treatment system.
Charles built the sewage system.
Charles trained as an engineer.
The toilet has two compartments, separating urine from other waste.
Urine-only flushing uses 2–3 deciliters [0.2–0.3 liters] of water.
Two greywater/urine cisterns provide 2 cubic meters [2,000 liters].
Shower and dishwasher water enter the greywater treatment tanks.
Bacteria die off while water stays in the tanks.
Centrifugal force separates toilet solids from blackwater liquid.
The separator needs emptying approximately every six months.
Incoming cistern water displaces an equal volume onward by gravity.
Drainage tubes are described as 30 centimeters [11.8 inches].
claims.doubt: The English subtitle gives no dimension qualifier, so depth, diameter and spacing cannot be distinguished.

claims.text: Greywater filters through the planted bed’s soil.
Wastewater fertilizes plants in the treatment bed.
More plants could be grown in the treatment bed.
The garden pond is the third treatment stage.
Pond bacteria levels are described as acceptable.
The pond has high E. coli levels.
claims.doubt: The automatic caption renders the organism as “EOL”; E. coli is a tentative reading, not a confirmed transcription.

claims.text: Pond water is not for drinking.
Pond samples have to be sent to a laboratory; they do that once a year or so.
The garden has an apple tree and a cherry tree.
Food compost is used for edible plants.
Composted toilet solids are used only for non-edible planting.
Separated toilet solids become a dry, dust-like residue.
Marie grew the tomatoes from seed with her four-year-old son.
The tomato plants grew a meter high [3.28 feet].
Indoor comfort varies with the season, including cold winter mornings.
No proposed solar heat-storage system has been purchased.
Further development needs money and time.
